messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 30-year-old carpenter married to his high school sweetheart, has been struggling with intrusive memories and intense emotional responses since he witnessed a traumatic event several months ago. One day at work, while installing cabinets in a client's home, John saw a man fall from the roof of an adjacent building. The impact was gruesome, leaving the victim with visible injuries that mirrored the aftermath of the accident. From that moment on, physical touch and specific tastes associated with the traumatic event have become potent triggers for John. The memory of what he witnessed comes back to him without warning, triggered by something as simple as a client's hand on his shoulder or the taste of a meal he had been eating during the event. When these memories return, they feel completely real, as if he is reliving every terrifying moment again. This full sensory experience leaves John feeling overwhelmed and disconnected from reality. Unable to articulate the frightening event through words, he often finds himself unable to explain his distress even when trying to talk about it with his wife. John's distress manifests in several ways. When confronted with a trigger, he overeats excessively, finding temporary relief in food that numbs the emotional pain for a brief moment. He also deliberately dissociates, zoning out and leaving his body as if watching from afar. To cope further, John actively avoids thinking about the event altogether, pushing it to the back of his mind whenever possible. The trauma has left John with profound negative appraisals about himself and his life. He feels that his life has been irrevocably destroyed by what he witnessed. The incident has also made him doubt his own resilience; he believes he can't rely on himself anymore, feeling permanently damaged by the event. These beliefs are reinforced whenever he relives the memory, which often happens in response to a trigger. John’s negative appraisals and intrusive memories have significantly impacted his daily life. His marriage feels strained as he isolates himself from his wife and struggles to engage in activities they once enjoyed together. At work, John has become more anxious around clients who initiate physical contact or during tasks where the taste of his lunch becomes a trigger, leading him to avoid certain jobs altogether. John’s overeating and deliberate dissociation have worsened these negative appraisals. The cycle seems insurmountable; every time he relives the traumatic event, it reinforces the belief that his life is destroyed and he has permanently changed for the worse. He finds himself caught in a vicious loop where triggers lead to intrusive memories, which then fuel his maladaptive coping strategies and deepen his negative beliefs. The culmination of these struggles finally led John to seek help after an incident at work where he had a panic attack during a task that involved touching metal surfaces associated with the traumatic event. He was certain that something needed to change but feared that nothing could ever heal the profound damage he felt inside. Despite this fear, John hopes that therapy might offer some relief and perhaps help him reclaim his life from the shadows of trauma. John's current state is one of deep distress, marked by a pervasive sense of hopelessness and anxiety about facing any potential triggers in his daily life. He is most afraid that these memories will continue to dominate his existence, leaving him trapped in an endless cycle of distress and despair. However, there remains a glimmer of hope that he can learn to manage his symptoms and regain some semblance of the life he once had.
